title: The standard algorithm: ones row, tens row, sum

standards.facet: Multiply multidigit whole numbers using a standard algorithm

script.title: The standard algorithm: ones row, tens row, sum

beats.say: Welcome! Today we learn the standard algorithm for multiplying bigger numbers. We begin with a product we can see: thirty-two times seventy-two.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Multiply $32\times 72$ with the standard algorithm. Write the ones row, the tens row, and the sum.

beats.say: Thirty-two times seventy-two means seventy-two rows with thirty-two in each row. Picture a rectangle, thirty-two wide and seventy-two tall. The number of unit squares inside, its area, is the product.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.meaning: The answer to a multiplication. Here it is the area of the rectangle.

beats.say: Seventy-two rows? That is way too many to count one at a time!
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Don't count. Split the number seventy-two by its places. The seven is in the tens place, so it is worth seventy. The two is in the ones place, so it is worth just two.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.meaning: A digit is worth the digit times its place. In $72$, the $7$ is in the tens place, worth $70$. The $2$ is in the ones place, worth $2$.

beats.say: So cut the rectangle into two pieces: a big block of seventy rows, and a thin strip of two rows.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Start with the thin strip. Two rows of thirty-two is thirty-two times two, which is sixty-four.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Now the big block: seventy rows of thirty-two. Thirty-two times seven is two hundred twenty-four. But these are seven tens, so every bit of it is ten times bigger.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: So seventy times thirty-two is just two hundred twenty-four with a zero on the end?
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Exactly! Ten times bigger slides every digit one place to the left, and that leaves a zero in the ones place. Two thousand two hundred forty.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Ten times bigger: every digit slides one place left, and a $0$ fills the ones place.

beats.say: Put the two pieces back together. Sixty-four plus two thousand two hundred forty is two thousand three hundred four.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Hold on to this picture. The thin strip and the big block are exactly the two rows of the standard algorithm.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Here is the standard algorithm. Write the top number, thirty-two. Under it write the bottom number, seventy-two, with ones under ones and tens under tens. Each column is worth ten times the column to its right.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Line up the places: ones under ones, tens under tens.

beats.say: Row one is the ones row. Multiply the top number by the ones digit, the two. Thirty-two times two is sixty-four.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Row two is the tens row. The tens digit is seven, but it really means seventy. So the tens row starts with a zero in the ones place. That zero says: nothing in the ones place, all tens.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Tens row: write a $0$ in the ones place first.

do.meaning: A zero that holds a place open so the other digits stay in their correct places.

beats.say: Next, multiply by the seven. Thirty-two times seven is two hundred twenty-four. Write those digits to the left of the zero.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Could I skip the zero and tuck two hundred twenty-four right under the sixty-four?
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Try it and see. The four would land in the ones column, worth four instead of forty. Every digit would come out ten times too small. The zero keeps every digit in its true place.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Always write the shift zero first. It keeps the tens row ten times as big.

beats.say: Last, add the two rows. We add column by column, starting at the ones.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Ones: four plus zero is four.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Tens: six tens plus four tens is ten tens. That is one hundred, so write zero and carry the one.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Hundreds: nothing plus two plus the carried one is three.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Thousands: just the two. Write it.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Two thousand three hundred four. It matches the rectangle: the strip plus the block.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Check with a round-number estimate. Thirty-two is about thirty, and seventy-two is about seventy. Thirty times seventy is two thousand one hundred. Our answer lands in the same neighborhood.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: I tried one by myself! I did thirty-two times seven, got two hundred twenty-four, and wrote it in the tens row without the zero. My sum was two hundred eighty-eight.
beats.speaker: learner

do.text: Champ's try: he left out the shift zero.

beats.say: Good news, Champ. There is a quick test that catches this mistake in seconds: estimate with round numbers. Thirty-two is close to thirty. Seventy-two is close to seventy.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Estimate first: it is quick!
Round: $32\approx 30$.
Round: $72\approx 70$.

beats.say: Thirty times seventy is three times seven, twenty-one, and two zeros: two thousand one hundred.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Two thousand one hundred! But I got two hundred eighty-eight. That is way too small.
beats.speaker: learner

do.text: $2{,}100$ and $288$ are far apart!

beats.say: Right. Leave out the shift and the tens row comes out ten times too small. Put the zero back: two hundred twenty-four times ten is two thousand two hundred forty.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Put the $0$ back.
No shift: the tens row is $10$ times too small.

beats.say: Now sixty-four plus two thousand two hundred forty is two thousand three hundred four, right next to our estimate.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: The tens row always ends in $0$. If it does not, the shift is missing.

beats.say: Case one: the ones digit is a one. Let's multiply seventeen times eighty-one.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Multiply $17\times 81$. Write the ones row, the tens row, and the sum.

beats.say: The ones row is the top number times the ones digit. One group of seventeen is just seventeen.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: That is a copy of the top number. Times one changes nothing, so can I skip this row?
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Do not skip it. It is still a real row, worth seventeen of the answer. Leave it out and the sum comes up seventeen short. When the ones digit is one, just copy the top number.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: A ones digit of $1$: the ones row is a copy of the top number. Still write it.

beats.say: Now the tens row. The tens digit is eight, so we multiply by eighty. Write the shift zero first.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Eight times seven is fifty-six. Write the six and carry the five. Eight times one is eight, plus the five is thirteen. So seventeen times eighty is one thousand three hundred sixty.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Add the rows: seventeen plus one thousand three hundred sixty is one thousand three hundred seventy-seven.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Check: seventeen is about twenty and eighty-one is about eighty. Twenty times eighty is sixteen hundred. We got thirteen seventy-seven, close and a little less, because we rounded seventeen up.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Case two: a zero at the end of the top number. Let's multiply four hundred eighty times forty-eight.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Multiply $480\times 48$. Write the ones row, the tens row, and the sum.

beats.say: Ones row. Start in the ones place: eight times zero is zero. Write the zero.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Next, eight times eight. Eight tens times eight is sixty-four tens. That is six hundreds and four tens. Write the four in the tens place, and carry the six to the hundreds column.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.meaning: When a product has two digits, write the ones digit and pass the other digit to the next column to be added there.

beats.say: So a carry is just the leftover that does not fit in this column!
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Exactly. Last, eight times four hundreds is thirty-two hundreds. Add the carried six hundreds to make thirty-eight hundreds. That is three thousand, eight hundred. The ones row is three thousand eight hundred forty.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Now the tens row. We multiply by forty, so the shift zero goes first, in the ones place.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Then the four times the zero in four-eighty. Four times zero is zero.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Two zeros side by side! Did I make a mistake?
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: No. They are two different zeros. One is the shift zero. The other comes from the zero in four-eighty. Both belong.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Four times eight is thirty-two. Write the two, carry the three. Four times four is sixteen, plus the three is nineteen. Write nineteen.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Here is a way to see it at a glance. Cover the zeros: forty-eight times four is one hundred ninety-two. Count the zeros you covered: one in four-eighty and one in the forty. Put two zeros back: nineteen thousand two hundred.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Cover the zeros, multiply, then put the zeros back: $192$ and two zeros is $19{,}200$.

beats.say: Add the rows. Three thousand eight hundred forty plus nineteen thousand two hundred is twenty-three thousand forty.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Check with an estimate. Four-eighty is about five hundred. Forty-eight is about fifty. Five hundred times fifty is twenty-five thousand, and our answer is close.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Case three: three digits on top, with carries in both rows. Let's multiply eight hundred forty-two times sixty-nine.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Multiply $842\times 69$. Write the ones row, the tens row, and the sum.

beats.say: Ones row. Multiply the top number by nine, one digit at a time, starting at the ones. Nine times two is eighteen.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Eighteen is one ten and eight ones. Write the eight. The one ten is carried over to the tens column.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Next is the four. I will add the carried one to the four first, so five, and then do nine times five.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Careful, Champ. The carry is already a product, it came from nine times two. If you add it first, you multiply it by nine a second time. First multiply, then add: nine times four is thirty-six, plus the carried one is thirty-seven.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Multiply the digit first. Add the carry after.

beats.say: Thirty-seven tens is three hundreds and seven tens. Write the seven, carry the three. Nine times eight is seventy-two, plus three is seventy-five. Write seventy-five.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The ones row is seven thousand five hundred seventy-eight.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Tens row. The tens digit is six, so multiply by sixty. Shift zero first. Then six times two is twelve: write the two, carry the one.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Six times four is twenty-four, plus the one is twenty-five. Write the five, carry the two. Six times eight is forty-eight, plus the two is fifty. Write fifty.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The tens row is fifty thousand five hundred twenty. Notice it ends in zero, as every tens row does.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Now add the rows, with carries. Ones: eight plus zero is eight. Tens: seven plus two is nine.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Hundreds: five plus five is ten. Write zero, carry one.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Thousands: seven plus zero plus the carried one is eight.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Ten thousands: just the five. The sum is fifty-eight thousand ninety-eight.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Estimate: eight hundred forty-two is about eight hundred, and sixty-nine is about seventy. Eight hundred times seventy is fifty-six thousand. We are close.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Now let me try one with all the tricks! Sixteen times forty-nine.
beats.speaker: learner

do.text: Multiply $16\times 49$. Write the ones row, the tens row, and the sum.

beats.say: Ones row. Nine times six is fifty-four: write four, carry five.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Nine times one is nine, plus five is fourteen. So the ones row is one hundred forty-four.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Spot on. Now the tens row, with the shift zero first.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Tens row: shift zero first.

beats.say: Zero first. Four times six is twenty-four: write four, carry two.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Four times one is four, plus two is six. So sixty-four with the zero is six hundred forty.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: One hundred forty-four plus six hundred forty is seven hundred eighty-four.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Now, how do you know it is right without redoing everything? Run four quick checks.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Four quick checks, no redoing!

beats.say: Check one: the tens row must end in zero. Six hundred forty does.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Check 1: the tens row ends in $0$.

beats.say: Check two: the tens row is always the bigger row. It holds at least ten copies of the top number, while the ones row holds at most nine. And six hundred forty is bigger than one hundred forty-four.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Check 2: the tens row is bigger than the ones row. At least $10$ copies of the top number, against at most $9$.

beats.say: Check three: the sum ends in the same digit as the ones row, because the tens row adds nothing in the ones place. One hundred forty-four ends in four, and so does seven hundred eighty-four.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Check 3: the sum's last digit matches the ones row's last digit.
The tens row adds $0$ in the ones place.

beats.say: Check four: estimate. Round forty-nine up to fifty. Sixteen times fifty is eight hundred. Our seven hundred eighty-four is just below, because forty-nine is just below fifty.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Check 4: round a number and estimate.

beats.say: Four checks, and each one takes only a few seconds!
beats.speaker: learner

do.text: Each check takes a few seconds.

beats.say: Here is the whole standard algorithm on one board.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: One. The ones row: the top number times the ones digit.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Ones row: the top number times the ones digit.

beats.say: Two. The tens row: top number times the tens digit, with a shift zero.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Tens row: the top number times the tens digit, with a $0$ in the ones place.

beats.say: Three. Add the rows, column by column, and carry when a column reaches ten.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Add the rows, and carry when a column reaches ten.

beats.say: Four: check! The tens row ends in zero, and it is the bigger row.
beats.speaker: learner

do.text: Check: the tens row ends in $0$ and is the bigger row.

beats.say: Five: the sum ends like the ones row, and an estimate lands close.
beats.speaker: learner

do.text: Check: the sum ends like the ones row, and an estimate lands close.

beats.say: That is it, Champ! Two rows, a sum, and quick checks.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Two rows, a sum, and a check: that is the standard algorithm.
